summary.summary: This is the REVISED, pre-approval version of Appendix A to North Northamptonshire's 2025/26 Annual Governance Statement (AGS), going to the Audit and Governance Committee. The Council judges its governance arrangements generally effective, providing a moderate level of assurance, with 71% of 13 tracked 2024/25 governance actions implemented during the year (page 21); the rest — timely closure of internal-audit actions, social-care/DSG financial sustainability, consistent safeguarding controls, and assurance over shared services/partnerships — carry forward as live risks for 2026/27. It notes an overall revenue overspend against the 2025/26 budget in demand-led adults' and children's social care, partially offset by earmarked reserves, though no monetary figures are given in this narrative document (page 9). Against the Draft appendix (queue E06000061-7f338f1e), this REVISED copy adds one short paragraph on the Corporate Scrutiny Committee's review of performance/budget-monitoring reports (page 9) but is otherwise near-identical in substance.

compliance.notes: Scored from the complete Executive pack of 10 February 2026 (TMSS cover report plus Appendices A-E) together with the General Fund Final Budget/MTFP/Capital Programme report and its Budget Book, which carries the Capital Investment Strategy at pp.111-131. The Council HAS a Housing Revenue Account — Appendix B para 5.18 describes HRA self-financing for the legacy Kettering and Corby stock with loans assigned to one fund or the other and an Item 8 charge between the General Fund and the HRA; Appendix C charges no MRP on HRA assets and budgets £1.000m of HRA loan repayment; para 6.1 budgets £3.3m of HRA debt interest; and the capital programme includes £61.665m of HRA capital expenditure. HRA-conditional requirements were therefore scored as applicable, and the Council is marked down on two of them (no separate HRA liability benchmark, LB-04; and a General-Fund-only financing-costs ratio with no HRA equivalent, PI-07). Strongest areas by some distance: the liability benchmark (Table 2 plus an Arlingclose chart to 2075 with all four balances), the treasury investment strategy and counterparty framework, and governance/practices — Appendix E is a full 62-page TMP1-TMP12 document with schedules, a role-by-role dealing authorisation matrix and named external providers, which most authorities never publish. Weakest area: the non-treasury/commercial family in the 5-page Appendix D, where proportionality is recited but never demonstrated, no ratio of commercial income to net revenue stream is produced, no monetary limit caps commercial property investment, and the specified/non-specified analysis is inconsistent with the long-dated instruments the TMSS approves. The separate HRA Budget 2026-27 report was not in the pack but suppresses nothing scored here.

gaps.evidence: Appendix B p.11 para 5.11 table and Budget Book p.131 Table 11: financing costs £10.4m/£10.1m/£10.1m/£10.0m/£9.9m; proportion of net revenue stream 2.96% / 2.33% / 2.18% / 2.05% / 1.89% (2025/26 forecast to 2029/30)

Appendix E TMP6 p.39 lists 'Net income from commercial and service investments to net revenue stream' among the prudential indicators the Council will cover in its annual strategy documents; Appendix D p.5 Table 5 gives rates of return (commercial property 4.69%) but not as a ratio to the net revenue stream

Appendix E TMP3 p.25 and Appendix B para 3.14 restate the substance of Prudential Code paras 51–53 (no borrowing to invest primarily for financial return; PWLB certification), but no document contains a compliance statement citing paragraphs 51 to 53

Cover report para 4.6 and Appendix E TMP3 p.24 recite the principle that 'the risks of the Council's commercial investments should be proportionate to the Council's overall capacity — ie that plausible losses could be absorbed in budgets or reserves without unmanageable detriment to local services'; Appendix D para 3.2 sets service-loan limits 'to ensure that total exposure to service loans remains proportionate to the size of the Council'; Appendix D p.5 Table 4 gives total investment exposure of £157.896m (31.3.25) falling to £34.691m (31.3.27)

Appendix D p.2 Table 1 approved limits on service loans — subsidiaries £2.000m, local businesses £1.000m, local charities £0.500m, employees £0.500m, other £0.500m; p.3 Table 2 approved limit on shares in subsidiaries £2.000m

findings.headline: Council faces significant deferred capital investment requirements while managing a large inherited estate from local government reorganisation
findings.detail: The council inherited a complex asset portfolio from predecessor councils in 2021 and faces multiple competing capital investment priorities including highways, council housing, school expansion, SEND provision, and digital infrastructure. These capital requirements must be balanced against the financial constraints and funding limitations acknowledged in section 1.9.3.
findings.matters: Large capital investment needs compete with debt repayment capacity and may constrain financial flexibility; the council's ability to fund these requirements while managing debt is relevant to lender assessment
findings.figures: Total estate: 1,779 sites, 1,261 properties, estimated value £980.855m. Capital priorities include highways, council housing, school expansion, SEND provision, accommodation for vulnerable children, digital infrastructure and EV infrastructure.
findings.quote: significant capital investment requirements, including investment in highways, council housing, school expansion and SEND provision, accommodation for vulnerable children, facilities for people with disabilities, digital infrastructure and electric vehicle infrastructure

findings.headline: Council acknowledges challenging financial environment and is relying on asset disposals and commercial income to support savings requirements
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it is operating in a challenging financial environment with continuing demand and cost pressures in adult social care and children's services. The asset management plan is framed as part of the financial strategy, with asset decisions expected to generate capital receipts, commercial income and revenue savings. Commercial property appraisals are planned for 2027–28 to identify low-return assets for disposal.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's financial strategy relies on asset sales actually happening as planned, and whether their commercial portfolio is genuinely performing or carrying underperforming assets
findings.figures: Commercial portfolio: 247 properties, £381.2m value, generating £14.2m forecast income for 2026. Low-return assets to be identified in 2027–28.
findings.quote: The Plan sits within a challenging financial environment for North Northamptonshire Council. The Council's budget and Medium Term Financial Plan identify continuing demand and cost pressures across core services, including adult social care and children's services, alongside the need to deliver savings, efficiencies and income generation over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Indicative Budget Timeline and Scrutiny Process
findings.headline: Two-thirds of the net budget (£281.8m of £437m) consists of demand-led and volatile services
findings.detail: Three service areas—Adult Social Care (£166.4m), Children's Trust (£88.7m), and Home to School Transport (£26.7m)—account for 65% of the general fund budget. These are explicitly identified as demand-led and among the most volatile budgets, meaning they are harder to control and more exposed to demographic or cost-of-living changes.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that a majority of the council's budget is exposed to volatile, demand-driven costs rather than discretionary spending that can be easily adjusted
findings.figures: Adult Social Care £166.4m, Children's Trust £88.7m, Home to School Transport £26.7m = £281.8m of £437m net budget (65%)
findings.quote: the following areas which are demand led budgets and therefore some of the most volatile budgets across the Council and have a net budget of £281.8m (65%) would be subject to detailed budget scrutiny

findings.paper_title: Indicative Budget Timeline and Scrutiny Process
findings.headline: HRA rent convergence policy begins April 2027: £1/week increases, rising to £2/week from April 2028
findings.detail: Government has reintroduced rent convergence, allowing HRA rents to increase beyond the standard CPI+1% formula. From April 2027, eligible properties below formula rent will rise by £1/week additional; from April 2028 this increases to £2/week. The policy continues until properties converge to formula rent.
findings.matters: This is a policy-driven change to HRA rent-setting that affects both HRA income and tenant affordability; it is outside council control
findings.figures: £1 per week from 1 April 2027; £2 per week from 1 April 2028
findings.quote: Rent convergence will begin on 1 April 2027 with an initial increase of £1 per week for eligible properties and from April 2028, the increase will rise to £2 per week until rents reach the formula rent level

findings.paper_title: Indicative Budget Timeline and Scrutiny Process
findings.headline: Inflationary pressures in children's and adult social services are already evident in 2026/27 and expected to continue
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies ongoing cost inflation within the Children's Trust and adult services as a budget pressure. These are already showing in the current year and are forecast to persist into 2027/28 and the medium term. These are demand-driven pressures.
findings.matters: These are structural cost pressures outside the council's direct control; they consume budget headroom and cannot be addressed through efficiency alone
findings.figures: Children's Trust contract sum is £88.7m (20% of net budget); Adult Social Care is £166.4m (38% of net budget)
findings.quote: the cost of inflationary increases within the Children's Trust and across adult services. which have been evident for 2026/27 to date and are expected to continue into future years
